chunks.title: Who is Ayush Yadav?
chunks.text: Ayush Yadav is an R&D Software Engineer II at Cadence Design Systems. He works on performance-critical systems, C++ performance engineering, distributed systems, agentic AI and developer tooling, with production wins on Apple, Google, Samsung and NVIDIA workloads.

chunks.title: What does Ayush focus on?
chunks.text: Ayush cares about end-to-end ownership: from low-level profiling and distributed-system design to polished, accessible product surfaces. His engineering principle is profile first — optimization without measurement is folklore.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: MAESTRO is a portable multi-agent platform Ayush built at Cadence: a conductor orchestrates 10 specialist AI agents across a 20-phase, human-gated workflow that carries an Xcelium engineering ticket from intake and root-cause analysis through fix, validation, review, regression and release. Measured across 22 Jiras, it cut ticket-resolution time by 45% and root-cause-analysis time by 55%, and it was selected for trade-secret protection.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI agents for performance and memory
chunks.text: For Cadence ChipStack AI, Ayush built multi-agent Python workflows on the OpenAI Agents SDK that profile Xcelium simulations and apply and verify performance and memory fixes, achieving a 31.3% simulation speedup on a validated benchmark. A deterministic-first re-architecture cut end-to-end runtime from 148.3 s to 76.8 s (1.93x) and analysis from 71.1 s to 18.0 s (3.9x). He also built the shared agent framework with typed state, checkpoint and resume, structured outputs and fallback recovery, plus a YAML-driven LLM-as-judge regression framework.

chunks.title: Regression triage and Perforce replay tooling
chunks.text: Ayush built a ~16K-line Xcelium regression system using rule-based classification, TF-IDF clustering, historical learning and LLM review to automate triage, regolds, waivers and verification; it processed 2,120 failures across 79 runs, 73% of them in runs by other engineers. He also built cross-stream Perforce replay tooling that derives each changelist's source stream and selectively syncs only the paths it touches, automating multi-changelist backports across release branches.

chunks.title: Xcelium performance engineering
chunks.text: On Cadence's Xcelium logic simulator, Ayush did profiling-driven C++ optimization delivering +18 to 19% simulation throughput and +13 to 14% RTL transform runtime, validated on Apple, Google, Samsung and NVIDIA designs. He built a reusable Top-N profiling library presented at the Cadence India Conference.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution. One ticket in, a production-ready fix out — a conductor and 10 AI agents carry an engineering ticket from intake to release, with humans at every risky gate. Category: Agentic AI × Engineering Workflow. MAESTRO (Multi-Agent Engineering System for Ticket Resolution & Orchestration) is a portable, IDE-agnostic multi-agent platform for Xcelium engineering tickets. A conductor drives a 20-phase, human-gated workflow and delegates each phase to one of 10 specialist agents — from intake and root-cause analysis through validation, review, regression and release. Measured across 22 Jiras, it cut ticket-resolution time by 45% and root-cause-analysis time by 55%. Built with team Mindsmiths for the Cadence AI Buildathon 2026. Impact: Ticket resolution: 45% faster; Root-cause analysis: 55% faster; Workflow: 20 phases · 5 gates; IP status: Trade secret.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution. Tech stack: LLMs, AI Agents, MCP, Python, Bash, Jira, Perforce, Undo/UDB.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: How MAESTRO was built. Problem: Resolving a simulator ticket is a manual relay across R&D, validation and documentation. Evidence is scattered across the issue tracker, email, logs, specs, source control, code review and tribal knowledge, and every handoff re-gathers context the previous person already had. Under pressure steps get skipped, and important-but-not-critical tickets age in the backlog. Challenge: Turn the whole ticket lifecycle into one coordinated, trustworthy workflow: keep a single source of truth across 20 phases, ground every conclusion in real evidence, keep engineers in control at the risky steps, and stay cheap enough to run on every ticket — inside whichever IDE the engineer already uses.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: How MAESTRO was built. Designed a conductor that owns the 20-phase flow and delegates each phase to one of 10 specialist agents: intake, triage, debug/RCA, fix, validation, docs, review, regression, release and a cross-cutting memory agent. Kept one shared analysis document as the source of truth: every phase reads and writes it, so context is captured once and a run can resume exactly where it stopped. Grounded the agents knowledge-first: an offline knowledge base is searched before anything goes online, and every resolved ticket is written back so the next run starts warm. Wired engineering systems in through MCP servers and scripts — issue tracking, source control, code review and a time-travel debugger that rewinds a recorded failure to the exact bad write instead of guessing forward from logs.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: How MAESTRO was built. Added five human approval gates and handed hours-long steps such as builds and regressions to the engineer, so nothing ships without sign-off and no model time is spent idling. Kept it cheap by design: the smallest capable model per phase, with mechanical steps scripted at zero LLM tokens — runs in Cursor, Claude Code or GitHub Copilot.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: MAESTRO engineering details. Conductor-led phase routing: One conductor owns routing across 20 phases and forks on classification — defects take a logs-first root-cause path, enhancements take a requirements-and-design path. Document-as-state resumption: The shared analysis document is the run's state, so any session can pick up exactly where the previous one stopped instead of replaying a chat history. Time-travel root-cause analysis: A recorded failing run is rewound to the instruction that wrote the bad value, so RCA works backwards from the effect rather than guessing forward from logs. Self-healing validation loop: A failing validation test routes the ticket back to debug (defects) or design (enhancements); nothing advances on a red test. 45% faster ticket resolution and 55% faster root-cause analysis, measured across 22 Jiras.

chunks.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
chunks.text: MAESTRO engineering details. Smallest capable model per phase; mechanical steps such as formatting, diffs and regression analysis run as scripts at zero LLM tokens. Builds and regressions are handed to the engineer behind a gate, so the model never waits hours on a build. MAESTRO treats a ticket as a symphony rather than a prompt: the conductor never does the work itself — it sequences specialists, enforces the gates and keeps one score, the shared analysis document, that every agent plays from. Trust comes from constraints rather than instructions: root-cause fixes only, five human approval gates, and verify-don't-guess — every conclusion is checked against real evidence before the next phase starts.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory. Multi-agent LLM workflows that profile Xcelium simulations, diagnose runtime and memory bottlenecks, and apply and verify the fixes. Category: Agentic AI × EDA Performance. A multi-agent LLM system for Cadence ChipStack AI that profiles Xcelium SystemVerilog simulations, diagnoses runtime and memory bottlenecks, and recommends, applies and verifies fixes — compiler flags, RTL recodes, garbage-collection and memory tuning — from an interactive terminal UI. It spans a performance agent, a memory agent, a shared workflow framework and a regression framework: ~37K lines of Python and 650+ tests. Impact: Simulation speedup: 31.3%; End-to-end run: 1.93× faster; Analysis phase: 3.9× faster; Codebase: ~37K lines · 650+ tests. Tech stack: Python, OpenAI Agents SDK, Pydantic, Jinja2, pytest, YAML, Xcelium, SystemVerilog.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: How ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents was built. Problem: Simulation performance and memory work is expert-heavy: engineers read profiler output, correlate hotspots with RTL, choose flags or recodes, then re-run and compare. Early agent versions routed every mechanical step through LLM tool calls, which made them slow — and let reports quote numbers the parser never produced. Challenge: Build agents that go from profiler data to a verified fix with no manual steps, while staying fast, grounded in parsed data, resumable across sessions and testable even though no two runs are identical. Built an 8-agent performance pipeline — intake, planning, a parallel compiler-flag audit / hardware clustering / pattern extraction, a 3-tier RTL recode, apply, then re-run and compare.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: How ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents was built. Built the memory agent: heap snapshots and call-stack profiling, peak detection, shared-library attribution with C++ demangling, RTL file-and-line citations, and garbage-collection experiments with before/after comparison. Re-architected both agents deterministic-first: intake, simulation runs and profile parsing moved out of LLM tool loops into Python, keeping the model for reasoning and fallback. Architected a shared framework on the OpenAI Agents SDK: graph-based orchestration of agent nodes, schema-versioned state with checkpoint/resume, strict structured outputs, recovery from malformed JSON and per-node fallback routing. Eliminated hallucinated figures by rendering report numbers in Python and giving the reporting agents no tools, so every number traces back to parsed profile data.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: How ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents was built. Designed a proof-of-concept regression framework that drives the real terminal UI over a pseudo-terminal: one YAML entry per testcase, and a checklist-based LLM judge that compares each report with a reviewed golden.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents engineering details. 3-tier RTL recode: A deterministic pattern-database match runs first, then a spec-driven LLM recode from a pluggable optimization registry, then a general LLM fallback — each tier only runs when the one before cannot help. Hardware-type hotspot clustering: Hotspots are grouped by hardware element type so one recode propagates to every peer in the cluster. Truncated-JSON recovery: A LIFO bracket stack completes cut-off LLM output, 7+ observed wrapper formats are unwrapped, and a repair pass runs before any corrective retry. Checklist LLM-as-judge: Instead of asking for a similarity score, the judge answers five narrow yes/no questions; the score is the fraction answered yes, so it is repeatable and names exactly what regressed. 31.3% simulation speedup on a validated benchmark run.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents engineering details. Deterministic-first rework, measured on a benchmark design: end-to-end 148.3 s → 76.8 s (1.93×) and analysis 71.1 s → 18.0 s (3.9×, five model turns → one). First prompt in under 3 ms instead of ~47 s, by asking intake questions in Python before any model turn. Judge input compacted by 71% through path normalization and JSON truncation. The memory analysis step took 71 s, but the parsing inside it took 84 ms — the rest was the model deciding to call tools and retyping data between them. Running the parsing in Python and giving the analyser zero tools made it 3.9× faster and hallucination-proof: an agent with no tools cannot fetch a number that isn't in the parsed data.

chunks.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
chunks.text: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents engineering details. Exact comparison fails every run of a non-deterministic agent, and a holistic similarity prompt still scores a regressed report around 90%. A five-question checklist judge scored a planted regression at 60% and named exactly the two corrupted aspects.

chunks.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
chunks.text: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering. Low-level optimization work delivering measurable throughput improvements on large real-world workloads. Category: Systems Performance. A multi-quarter performance engineering effort on Cadence's Xcelium logic simulator, focused on profiling-driven optimization, RTL transformations and structured diagnostics for production customer workloads. Impact: Simulation throughput: +18–19%; RTL transform runtime: +13–14%; Debug RCA time: ~40% faster; Customer-impacting: Multi-million-$ Samsung deal. Tech stack: C++, SystemVerilog, Valgrind, AddressSanitizer, Perforce.

chunks.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
chunks.text: How Xcelium Logic Simulator was built. Problem: Customer designs of increasing scale stress simulator throughput. Even small inefficiencies in hot paths compound across millions of simulation events, costing engineering hours and infrastructure. Challenge: Identify high-leverage bottlenecks across an industrial simulation engine, reason rigorously about runtime behavior, and ship low-risk C++ changes that move the needle on production workloads. Built a reusable C++ performance-analysis library enabling Top-N profiling and structured diagnostics, presented at Cadence India Conference. Used Valgrind, AddressSanitizer and runtime profilers to isolate hotspots in critical simulation paths. Implemented RTL transformations in the Xform Engine that reshape designs into more simulator-friendly forms.

chunks.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
chunks.text: How Xcelium Logic Simulator was built. Validated improvements against designs from Apple, Google, Samsung and NVIDIA on representative workloads.

chunks.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
chunks.text: Xcelium Logic Simulator engineering details. Top-N hotspot profiling: A reusable C++ performance-analysis library ranks the hottest call paths so optimization effort targets the highest-leverage code (presented at Cadence India Conference). RTL transformation passes: The Xform Engine reshapes designs into more simulator-friendly forms before execution. +18–19% simulation throughput on representative customer workloads. +13–14% RTL transform runtime improvement. Hotspots isolated with Valgrind, AddressSanitizer and runtime profilers; changes kept small and low-risk for production. Validated against Apple, Google, Samsung and NVIDIA designs. Performance work on an industrial simulator is dominated by measurement discipline: a structured Top-N profiling library made hot paths visible and repeatable so every change could be attributed to a concrete win.

chunks.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
chunks.text: Xcelium Logic Simulator engineering details. Optimizations shipped as small, low-risk C++ changes validated on representative real-world designs rather than micro-benchmarks.

chunks.title: AlgoLens — Interactive DSA Platform
chunks.text: How AlgoLens was built. Problem: Algorithm learning resources tend to be static. Understanding behavior under different inputs, replaying state and exporting visuals for teaching are awkward at best. Challenge: Build a fluid, accessible, GPU-friendly visualization engine that handles 60+ algorithms with a unified step model, deterministic replay, video export and AI-assisted understanding — held to product-grade quality bars. Designed a step-based execution model with deterministic replay across all algorithms. Built Canvas-based renderers with smooth, reduced-motion-aware animations. Integrated FFmpeg-WASM for in-browser video export of execution traces. Layered GenAI for natural-language explanations and complexity analysis. Implemented exact, fuzzy, phonetic and semantic search for algorithm discovery.

chunks.title: AlgoLens — Interactive DSA Platform
chunks.text: How AlgoLens was built. Hardened with WCAG 2.1 AA, Sentry, Web Vitals, Playwright, Storybook, Percy and CI quality gates.

chunks.title: AlgoLens — Interactive DSA Platform
chunks.text: AlgoLens engineering details. Step-based execution model: Every algorithm emits a uniform stream of inspectable steps, enabling deterministic replay and scrubbing across 60+ algorithms. Deterministic replay: Given the same input and seed, a run reproduces exactly — essential for teaching and reliable video export. Multi-modal search: Exact, fuzzy, phonetic and semantic search over the algorithm catalogue for fast discovery. Canvas renderers with reduced-motion-aware animations keep visualizations GPU-friendly. In-browser FFmpeg-WASM export avoids any server round-trip for video. Held to WCAG 2.1 AA with Sentry, Web Vitals, Playwright and CI quality gates. The unifying idea is a single step model: by forcing every algorithm to express itself as a sequence of inspectable steps, replay, export and AI explanations all become generic features instead of per-algorithm work.

chunks.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.text: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System. A ~16K-line system that turns thousands of regression failures into safe, verified actions — regold, filter, waive or escalate. Category: Developer Tooling × Automation. After a simulator change, regression campaigns return hundreds to thousands of failing test/mode combinations, and each one needs a decision. This ~16K-line system automates triage, regolds, waivers and verification using rule-based classification, TF-IDF clustering, historical learning and an optional LLM review. It has processed 2,120 failures across 79 runs — 73% of them in runs by other engineers. Impact: Failures processed: 2,120; Regression runs: 79; Run by other engineers: 73%; Codebase: ~16K lines. Tech stack: Bash, Python, scikit-learn, Perforce, LLMs, Xcelium.

chunks.source: Projects · Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.text: How Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System was built. Problem: Every failing test needs one of several actions: update the golden file, add a diff filter, ignore or waive it, repair the workspace, or escalate. The evidence changes from run to run (addresses, PIDs, timestamps, paths), one root cause produces dozens of near-identical failures, and a wrong regold silently blinds the suite to a real defect. Challenge: Automate the decision safely: recognise the same fault across runs, never let a crash or tool error become the new golden, handle modes that compare against different golden files, verify every change per mode and learn from past campaigns — while staying resumable and undoable. Normalised regression and nightly failure lists into test, bank and mode sets, then re-ran each mode in parallel with per-file locks, dry-run, resume and undo.

chunks.source: Projects · Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.text: How Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System was built. Canonicalised evidence into run-stable signatures by masking addresses, numbers, paths, PIDs and timestamps, so repeats of one fault share a fingerprint. Categorised every failure with rules, a weighted vote over recent runs and saved human corrections, then grouped similar failures with TF-IDF and agglomerative clustering. Gated disposition by class: only diff-class failures can ever reach a golden file — crashes, timeouts and tool errors always go to root-cause analysis. Verified every regold with a per-mode rerun, and emitted diff filters, IGNORE files or waivers where a regold was not the right answer. Added an optional LLM review (JEDAI) that checks each diff against the pending code change and flags tests that must not be regolded — advisory only, it can never relax the gate.

chunks.source: Projects · Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.text: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System engineering details. Run-stable failure signatures: Error text, diff lines and backtraces are masked and hashed separately, so two copies of the same fault land on the same fingerprint even when addresses and timestamps differ. Precedence-ordered categorisation: A live human correction beats saved corrections, which beat a weighted historical vote, which beats the rule-based class. Within-class TF-IDF clustering: Failures are clustered only inside their class — strictest for crashes — so one root cause is reviewed once instead of dozens of times. 2,120 failures handled across 79 runs; 73% of them in runs by engineers other than the author. 148 crash and tool-error failures kept away from golden files by the class gate. Parallel execution sized to CPU and memory, with per-testcase and per-golden-file locks.

chunks.source: Projects · Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
chunks.text: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System engineering details. Mistakes here are lopsided: accepting a real regression as golden blinds the suite to that defect for good, while refusing a valid change only costs time. So a deterministic control plane stays in charge, and the LLM is strictly an advisor.

chunks.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
chunks.text: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay. Backport a multi-changelist fix to any release stream in one command — syncing only the paths those changelists touch. Category: Developer Tooling × Release Engineering. A fix on the development stream usually has to be reproduced on every supported release stream, often as several changelists — the source change, its regolds and a new test. This tooling derives each changelist's source stream, selectively syncs only the paths the changelists touch, merges them in order and reports exactly which files still need a manual resolve, automating multi-CL backports across Xcelium release branches. Impact: Input: CL numbers + target; Sync scope: Touched paths only; Mixed-origin CLs: Supported; Tooling: ~1.6K lines. Tech stack: Perforce, Bash, csh, Linux.

chunks.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
chunks.text: How Cross-Stream Perforce Replay was built. Problem: Backports were done by hand, one changelist at a time, in hand-prepared workspaces. Partial client views meant missing paths surfaced one failure at a time, a full sync was too expensive, the origin stream of each changelist was often unknown, and auto-resolve reported one aggregate status that hid the files it declined to merge. Challenge: Derive every operand from changelist metadata — the origin stream, which paths must exist in the workspace, and the merge order — so the engineer supplies only changelist numbers and a target branch. Detected the source stream of every changelist from its files, so one run can mix changelists from different streams, and printed the map before merging. Built the sync plan from only the files and directories those changelists touch, instead of syncing the whole tree.

chunks.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
chunks.text: How Cross-Stream Perforce Replay was built. Repaired workspace faults automatically — extending the client view for out-of-view paths and recovering clobbered writable files — then retried. Merged changelists in ascending order, each from its own stream at its own revision, so any failure points at exactly one changelist. Ran a single auto-resolve at the end and listed the declined files for manual resolve; nothing is ever submitted automatically. Optionally created a disposable target workspace with only the project configuration synced, and reported the teardown command.

chunks.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
chunks.text: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay engineering details. Changelist-derived working set: The paths that must exist in the workspace are derived from the changelists themselves rather than declared up front in a client view. Ordered point-in-time integration: Changelists merge in ascending order, each from its own origin stream at exactly its own revision, so unrelated work in between is never carried across. Resolve partitioning: One auto-resolve after all merges, split into 'merged cleanly' and 'declined', so the files that need a human are always named. A recorded run replayed two changelists — six source files, a new three-file testcase and 32 golden files — to a release stream in one call, and named the 32 files that needed a manual resolve. Only changelist-touched paths are synced, so a replay never pays for a full-tree sync.

chunks.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
chunks.text: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay engineering details. Most backport tooling reads a path and throws away everything else. Here the path, the operation, the origin stream and the changelist number together define the working copy that has to exist before the merge can even start.

chunks.title: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis
chunks.text: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis. A 60 FPS computer-vision coaching system that scores exercise form with deterministic feedback loops. Category: Computer Vision × ML Product. PostureIQ is an ML-powered posture and form-coaching system built around real-time pose estimation, temporal smoothing, confidence gating and rep-quality scoring for exercise feedback. Impact: Frame rate: 60 FPS; Accuracy: >95%; Quality: pytest · golden traces · CLI. Tech stack: Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe, BlazePose, NumPy, pytest.

chunks.title: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis
chunks.text: How PostureIQ was built. Problem: Exercise-form feedback is usually delayed, subjective or dependent on a trainer being present. A useful assistant needs to infer pose continuously and provide clear feedback without jitter or false positives. Challenge: Maintain real-time capture, inference and rendering while making noisy pose landmarks stable enough for actionable coaching and automated quality scoring. Built a deterministic capture-to-infer-to-render loop with OpenCV and MediaPipe/BlazePose. Added temporal smoothing, Kalman filtering, confidence gating, adaptive thresholds and 3D landmark checks to reduce noisy corrections. Implemented rep-quality scoring around ROM, tempo and symmetry with audio/visual feedback cues. Instrumented FPS, latency and error telemetry with dashboards for repeatable performance analysis.

chunks.title: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis
chunks.text: How PostureIQ was built. Added pytest coverage, golden traces and a CLI for reproducible validation runs.

chunks.title: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis
chunks.text: PostureIQ engineering details. Pose estimation (BlazePose): Real-time landmark inference from the webcam feed via MediaPipe/BlazePose. Kalman filtering & temporal smoothing: Noisy per-frame landmarks are stabilized so coaching feedback doesn't jitter or fire false corrections. Rep-quality scoring: Range-of-motion, tempo and symmetry are combined into a single actionable form score. 60 FPS capture → infer → render loop. >95% reported accuracy with confidence gating and adaptive thresholds. FPS, latency and error telemetry instrumented for repeatable analysis. The hard part of pose coaching isn't detection but trust: confidence gating, Kalman smoothing and 3D landmark checks turn noisy per-frame estimates into stable, actionable feedback.

chunks.title: Track Person App — Movement Tracking & Visualization
chunks.text: How Track Person App was built. Problem: Movement data is hard to reason about from raw coordinates alone; users need a visual trail and a clean data model for location events. chunks.title: System design · URL Shortener
chunks.text: URL Shortener: Map long URLs to short codes and redirect at scale (bit.ly-style). Requirements: Generate a unique short code per long URL. Redirect short → long with very low latency. Handle a very high read:write ratio (reads ≫ writes). Optional analytics, expiry and custom aliases. Components: API service — Validates input, creates or looks up mappings.; Key generation — Base62 of an auto-increment id or hash, collision-checked.; KV store / DB — code → long-URL mapping, sharded by code.; Cache (Redis) — Hot short-codes for sub-millisecond redirects.; CDN / edge — Caches redirects close to users.. Trade-offs: 301 (permanent, cacheable, loses analytics) vs 302 (temporary, countable). Hashing (stateless, collisions) vs counter+Base62 (coordination, no collisions). A read-through cache adds complexity but is essential at this read ratio.

chunks.title: System design · Rate Limiter
chunks.text: Rate Limiter: Protect services by capping request rate per client. Requirements: Limit N requests per window per key (user / IP / API key). Low latency with a clear fail-open or fail-closed policy. Work across many app servers consistently. Return 429 with a Retry-After hint. Components: Limiter middleware — Checks and decrements quota before handling.; Counter store (Redis) — Atomic counters/tokens keyed by client + window.; Algorithm — Token bucket, sliding-window log or fixed window.; Policy — Per-tier limits and burst allowance.. Trade-offs: Fixed window (cheap, boundary bursts) vs sliding window (accurate, costlier). Token bucket allows bursts; leaky bucket smooths output. Local in-memory (fast, per-node) vs centralized (consistent, network hop).

chunks.title: System design · Job Scheduler
chunks.text: Job Scheduler: Run tasks reliably — now, delayed or recurring. Requirements: Enqueue jobs with priority and a run-at time. At-least-once execution with retries and backoff. Scale workers horizontally. Visibility into pending, running, failed and done jobs. Components: Queue / broker — Durable job queue (SQS / Kafka / DB table).; Scheduler — Moves due delayed/cron jobs into the ready queue.; Workers — Pull jobs, execute, ack or retry.; Dead-letter queue — Captures jobs that exhaust retries.; Store — Job state, idempotency keys and results.. Trade-offs: At-least-once + idempotency (simple, needs dedupe) vs exactly-once (hard). Push vs pull worker models. Priority queues vs FIFO fairness.

chunks.title: System design · Log Analytics System
chunks.text: Log Analytics System: Ingest, index and query high-volume logs. Requirements: Ingest millions of events per second. Full-text and structured search. Time-windowed aggregations and dashboards. Retention tiers and archival. Components: Collectors / agents — Ship logs from hosts.; Ingest pipeline (Kafka) — Buffer with back-pressure.; Index (Elasticsearch) — Searchable inverted index.; Object storage — Cheap cold / archival tier.; Query / dashboard — Search and visualize.. Trade-offs: Index everything (fast queries, costly) vs sample / schema-on-read. Hot / warm / cold tiering for cost control.

chunks.title: System design · Simulation Regression Dashboard
chunks.text: Simulation Regression Dashboard: Track pass/fail trends across nightly simulation runs. Requirements: Ingest results from thousands of regression tests. Separate new failures from flaky and known failures. Trend pass-rate over time with per-test history. Drill into logs and artifacts of a failure. Components: Run ingest — Parse results from CI / sim farm.; Results DB — Per-test, per-run status and metadata.; Flake detector — Classifies intermittent failures.; Dashboard — Trends, diffs and owners.; Artifact store — Logs and waveforms linked per failure.. Trade-offs: Store all artifacts (debuggable, large) vs fetch on demand. Real-time vs batch aggregation.

chunks.title: System design · Waveform Compression System
chunks.text: Waveform Compression System: Compress digital simulation waveforms for storage and fast replay. Requirements: Compress huge value-change dumps (VCD/FSDB-style). Random-access replay at any time point. Lossless for digital signals. Fast writes during simulation. Components: Value-change capture — Records signal transitions, not samples.; Delta + RLE encoding — Stores changes and run-lengths.; Dictionary / bit-packing — Packs enum / bus values tightly.; Chunked index — Time-indexed blocks for seeking.; Reader — Decompresses windows on demand.. Trade-offs: Event-based (compact for sparse activity) vs sampled. Bigger blocks compress better but slow random access.
